title: The Jagirdar's Son Who Read Kings

title_i18n.en: The Jagirdar's Son Who Read Kings

subtitle: From Sasaram’s dust to Jaunpur’s books, a jagirdar’s son studies how kingdoms breathe
era: Early life and Bihar service, c. 1472-1528 CE
moral: Discipline learned early can shape a lifetime of power.

sources.citation: Abbas Khan Sarwani, Tarikh-i-Sher Shahi, c. 1580/1586
sources.note: Main narrative for Farid's childhood, Jaunpur education, Sasaram estate management and the tiger-name tradition.
Later Mughal-era chronological cross-check for Sher Khan's Bihar rise.

sources.citation: K.R. Qanungo, Sher Shah and His Times (1965); Satish Chandra, Medieval India, Part II (2007 ed.)
sources.note: Modern critical synthesis of the early biography and its single-source limits.

panels.shot: dramatic mid-shot from slightly low angle

dialogue.text: In Lodi Hindustan, an Afghan jagirdar’s son named Farid reads kings in books and in fields, long before the world will call him Sher Shah.

panels.shot: wide shot of Sasaram landscape at dawn

dialogue.text: Sasaram, in the shadow of the Kaimur hills. Here, sometime in the late fifteenth century, a son is born to Hasan Khan Sur, an Afghan jagirdar of the Lodi sultans.

panels.shot: intimate interior mid-shot

dialogue.text: The jagir brings land, dues and quarrels. In the small Sur household, talk of arrears, rival Afghans and Lodi officers fills the night air more than lullabies.

panels.shot: close-up on Farid’s attentive face

dialogue.text: Abbas Khan Sarwani, writing later for Akbar, will say that even as a boy, Farid listened more to accounts than to praise. He watched how money bent men, and how land bound them.

panels.shot: wide shot of a Jaunpur madrasa courtyard

dialogue.text: From the small town of Sasaram, Farid is sent to Jaunpur, the ‘Shiraz of Hind’, to learn Persian letters and the culture of rule that flows from Delhi and beyond.

panels.shot: over-the-shoulder close-up on manuscript

dialogue.text: Sarwani’s Tarikh remembers him steeped in Persian histories and letters, absorbing not only stories of kings but the etiquettes, decrees and records that gave those stories weight.

panels.shot: medium shot of teacher and Farid

dialogue.speaker: farid_khan
dialogue.text: Master, what is a king without knowing who tills each field?

panels.shot: transitional montage-style wide shot

dialogue.text: Outside the madrasa, the Lodi Sultanate strains. Afghan nobles jostle for jagirs, governors grow unruly, and new powers watch from Bengal and the Deccan. Jaunpur hums with rumours of court and campaign.

panels.shot: mid-shot of Farid receiving a letter

dialogue.text: Then comes the summons. Hasan Khan’s jagir in Bihar—Sasaram and Khawaspur-Tanda—needs firmer hands. Whether through neglect or rivalry, the Sur estates are said to be fraying.

panels.shot: long shot of Farid riding through countryside

dialogue.text: Farid leaves the city of books for the fields of his father. Between Jaunpur’s arcades and Sasaram’s soil, he will try to weave learning into practice.

panels.shot: wide shot of Sasaram jagir offices

dialogue.text: Sarwani paints a clear picture: the young Farid surveys his father’s jagir, studies each village, summons oppressive collectors and softened peasants, and begins to test what justice can do for revenue.

panels.shot: bird’s-eye view over fields and boundaries

dialogue.text: He is said to measure fields himself, to fix demand not by guess but by land and harvest. To reward honest men, to restrain greedy ones, and to secure the cultivator so that he stays.

panels.shot: medium shot near village edge

dialogue.speaker: farid_khan
dialogue.text: If we break the plough, what will we rule over tomorrow?

panels.shot: low-angle medium shot of Farid confronting officials

dialogue.text: In Sarwani’s telling, he rebukes corrupt men without fear, even when they are his father’s followers. Discipline, not favour, will anchor the estate—and, he believes, any kingdom.

panels.shot: mid-shot of Farid listening to peasants

dialogue.text: The chronicle remembers cultivators finding in him a patron, and revenue rising as fields once abandoned are sown again. Whether embellished or exact, the pattern foreshadows the Sur ruler he will be.

panels.shot: dynamic hunting-scene wide shot, but with emphasis on uncertainty

dialogue.text: Later, Sarwani will explain his title 'Sher' with a tale of a tiger hunt and royal praise. The epithet is sure, the exact hunt less so—memory and legend mingling on the page.

panels.shot: wide shot of Bihar landscape with multiple powers

dialogue.text: Beyond Sasaram, Bihar is a chessboard of Afghan chiefs, Lodi officers and neighbouring sultans. In this contested land, Farid’s small jagir becomes his training ground in the larger game.

panels.shot: medium shot of Farid in simple court at Bihar

dialogue.text: As his management strengthens the estate, other Afghan leaders in Bihar take note. Nizamuddin’s Tabaqat later places him among those rising in the region, a young man whose care for accounts hints at larger ambitions.

panels.shot: close-up of Farid at night with lamp and ledger

dialogue.text: Between lines of Firdausi and lines of land, he studies how rulers rose and fell. Sarwani, writing under Akbar, will frame these Bihar years as the forge where Farid learned to rule men through order.

panels.shot: wide, contemplative shot of Farid overlooking fields at sunset

dialogue.text: Before he contests sultans and emperors, Farid masters a smaller realm—books, estates and men in Bihar. It is here that the jagirdar’s son first tests the discipline that will later shape Hindustan.
